options.a: Near-simultaneous sedation and neuromuscular blockade to facilitate intubation in at-risk patients
options.b: Paralysis first, then a sedative once tube placement is confirmed so induction does not drop the BP
options.c: Awake intubation with topical anesthesia and light sedation, avoiding a paralytic so breathing continues
options.d: Sedation alone titrated to tolerate laryngoscopy, with the paralytic held back for a failed first attempt

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the RSI sequence: a paralytic given before the induction agent leaves the patient awake and paralyzed.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes an awake/topicalized intubation technique; RSI by definition pairs an induction agent with a paralytic.
distractorExplanations.d: That is sedation-facilitated intubation; RSI gives the paralytic immediately after induction, not as a rescue drug.

options.a: Direct visualization of the tube passing the cords, with capnography reserved for difficult intubations
options.b: Waveform capnography plus clinical assessments (bilateral breath sounds, chest rise)
options.c: A colorimetric ETCO2 detector alone, which also tracks tube position continuously during transport
options.d: Pulse oximetry rising within 30 seconds plus breath sounds, which reliably excludes esophageal placement

distractorExplanations.a: Seeing the tube pass the cords can be wrong or the tube can move; waveform capnography is expected for every intubation.
distractorExplanations.c: Colorimetric detectors give a one-time color change and cannot monitor continuously; dislodgement en route would be missed.
distractorExplanations.d: SpO2 lags for minutes after preoxygenation, so a normal reading does not exclude an esophageal tube; capnography does.

options.a: Two failed intubation attempts while SpO2 stays above 94% with BVM ventilation
options.b: Severe facial trauma in a child under 10 years old who needs a definitive airway
options.c: Cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate scenarios require a front-of-neck airway
options.d: Status asthmaticus with poor air movement, before any attempt at BVM or intubation

distractorExplanations.a: If BVM still oxygenates (SpO2 above 94%), this is cannot-intubate-CAN-oxygenate: use an SGA/BVM, not a surgical cric.
distractorExplanations.b: Surgical cricothyrotomy is generally contraindicated in young children (small cricothyroid membrane); needle cric is used.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong timing: front-of-neck access is the last step of the failed-airway algorithm, never a first move in asthma.

options.a: 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 4th/5th ICS mid/anterior axillary
options.b: 2nd ICS midclavicular line, inserting the needle along the inferior border of the 2nd rib
options.c: 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line, directly over the nipple on the affected side
options.d: Subxiphoid, angled toward the left shoulder, the same approach used for pericardiocentesis

distractorExplanations.b: Needle goes over the superior border of the 3rd rib; the intercostal artery, vein, and nerve run under each rib.
distractorExplanations.c: The 5th ICS midclavicular site lies over the heart on the left; lateral sites use the mid/anterior axillary line.
distractorExplanations.d: Subxiphoid toward the left shoulder is the pericardiocentesis landmark for tamponade, not pleural decompression.

options.a: Confirm ROSC when ETCO2 drops suddenly below 10 mm Hg during compressions
options.b: Indicate CPR quality and early ROSC (sudden ETCO2 rise)
options.c: Decide on shocks by showing whether the rhythm is VF or pulseless VT
options.d: Titrate ventilations upward until ETCO2 falls below 20 mm Hg

distractorExplanations.a: Direction is reversed: ROSC shows as an abrupt ETCO2 rise (often to 35–45); a fall below 10 signals poor CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Rhythm and shock decisions come from the ECG/monitor; capnography reflects perfusion and ventilation, not rhythm.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilating to a low ETCO2 raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts coronary perfusion; ETCO2 under 10 means weak CPR.

options.a: A non-rebreather mask kept on the face at 15 L/min during laryngoscopy
options.b: Rapid BVM ventilation at 20+ breaths/min between paralysis and laryngoscopy
options.c: High-flow nasal oxygen during apnea to prolong safe apnea time
options.d: Holding all oxygen until the tube is placed, to avoid absorption atelectasis

distractorExplanations.a: A face mask has to come off for laryngoscopy, so it cannot deliver oxygen during apnea; a nasal cannula stays on.
distractorExplanations.b: Aggressive bagging after paralysis insufflates the stomach and raises aspiration risk; apneic oxygenation is passive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a minor theoretical concern with practice; withholding oxygen shortens safe apnea time and speeds desaturation.

options.a: Immediate blind finger sweeps and back blows, as for a foreign-body obstruction
options.b: Nebulized racemic epinephrine first-line, the same treatment used for croup stridor
options.c: Immediate needle cricothyrotomy before any attempt at positive-pressure ventilation
options.d: High-quality BVM with jaw thrust/CPAP pressure and progressive advanced measures

distractorExplanations.a: Treats laryngospasm like a choking FBAO; blind sweeps are not recommended and back blows do not open closed cords.
distractorExplanations.b: Racemic epinephrine treats subglottic edema in croup; laryngospasm is reflex cord closure broken by pressure/jaw thrust.
distractorExplanations.c: Skips the sequence: most laryngospasm resolves with jaw thrust and CPAP/BVM pressure; surgical access is the last resort.

options.a: Relative difficulty of laryngoscopy based on oropharyngeal structures visible
options.b: Glottic view during direct laryngoscopy, graded from full cords to epiglottis only
options.c: Thyromental distance as a predictor of difficult bag-mask ventilation
options.d: Risk of difficult BVM from beard, obesity, age, and no teeth (MOANS)

distractorExplanations.b: That is the Cormack-Lehane grade, seen during laryngoscopy; Mallampati is assessed beforehand with the mouth open.
distractorExplanations.c: Thyromental distance is part of the LEMON 3-3-2 evaluation, and Mallampati predicts laryngoscopy, not BVM difficulty.
distractorExplanations.d: MOANS is the mnemonic for difficult bag-mask ventilation; Mallampati grades visible oropharyngeal structures.

options.a: Securing a definitive tube on the next attempt before switching to rescue devices
options.b: Oxygenation/ventilation—rescue devices and front-of-neck access if needed
options.c: Immediate surgical cricothyrotomy after the first failed attempt, even if BVM works
options.d: Passing a bougie blindly on repeated attempts until SpO2 falls below 80%

distractorExplanations.a: Prioritizes the tube over oxygen; repeated attempts cause edema and hypoxia, so failed airways move to SGA/BVM first.
distractorExplanations.c: If BVM or an SGA oxygenates, the patient is not CICO; front-of-neck access is reserved for cannot-oxygenate situations.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for SpO2 to fall before stopping attempts is backwards; attempts are limited and oxygenation is restored first.

options.a: Suction set up after the first attempt, since secretions are rarely present in fasting patients
options.b: A single preferred blade size, with backup devices left in the ambulance to keep the scene uncluttered
options.c: Equipment readiness for failed airway (BVM, suction, extraglottic/surgical backup) and confirmation plan
options.d: Preoxygenation for 30 seconds by BVM at 30 breaths/min, followed directly by laryngoscopy

distractorExplanations.a: EMS airway patients are not fasting and often vomit; suction must be running and ready before the first look.
distractorExplanations.b: Backups stored in the ambulance are not ready; failed-airway gear (SGA, other blade, cric kit) must be at the head.
distractorExplanations.d: Preoxygenation takes about 3 minutes (or 8 vital-capacity breaths), not 30 seconds of rapid bagging into the stomach.

options.a: Arterial oxygen saturation, replacing the need for a pulse oximeter after intubation
options.b: Correct tube depth, showing whether the tip sits above the carina or in a mainstem bronchus
options.c: Exact PaCO2, since ETCO2 equals arterial CO2 in shock and cardiac arrest
options.d: Tracheal placement and ongoing ventilation effectiveness/CO2 elimination

distractorExplanations.a: Capnography measures exhaled CO2, not oxygenation; SpO2 monitoring is still required after intubation.
distractorExplanations.b: A right mainstem tube still produces a normal waveform; depth is checked by breath sounds, tube marking, and imaging.
distractorExplanations.c: ETCO2 underestimates PaCO2, and the gap widens in shock and arrest because of reduced pulmonary blood flow.

options.a: Allowing adequate expiratory time and avoiding excessive rates that cause auto-PEEP
options.b: Rates of 20–24 breaths/min with large tidal volumes to blow off retained CO2
options.c: A short expiratory time with a 1:1 I:E ratio to keep minute ventilation high
options.d: Permissive hypoxia, keeping SpO2 near 85% to protect the hypoxic drive

distractorExplanations.b: Fast rates and big volumes shorten exhalation and stack breaths, causing auto-PEEP, hypotension, and pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.c: Obstructive disease needs a long exhalation (I:E of 1:4 or more); a 1:1 ratio traps air with every breath.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the COPD hypoxic-drive teaching with asthma; status asthmaticus needs oxygen, and the tolerated value is CO2.

options.a: Intubation fails twice but an SGA gives good chest rise
options.b: You cannot oxygenate/ventilate and cannot intubate (CICO)
options.c: A child with epiglottitis is drooling but holds SpO2 at 95%
options.d: As the first step for a snoring airway before a jaw thrust

distractorExplanations.a: An SGA that ventilates means the patient can be oxygenated; continue with the SGA rather than cutting the neck.
distractorExplanations.c: A child who is oxygenating should be kept calm and transported; instrumenting the airway can trigger full obstruction.
distractorExplanations.d: Snoring is partial upper-airway obstruction fixed by positioning, jaw thrust, and adjuncts long before surgical access.

options.a: Increases preload by pushing blood from the lungs into the left atrium
options.b: Causes vasodilation through hyperoxia-induced nitric oxide release
options.c: Increases intrathoracic pressure and may reduce venous return
options.d: Triggers a vagal reflex that slows the heart below 50 beats/min

distractorExplanations.a: Positive pressure lowers venous return to the right heart, so overall preload falls rather than rises.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperoxia tends to cause vasoconstriction; the BP drop comes from raised intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return.
distractorExplanations.d: PPV-related hypotension is a preload problem from intrathoracic pressure, not a vagal bradycardia reflex.

options.a: ST elevation meeting criteria in anatomically contiguous leads
options.b: Diffuse ST elevation in nearly all leads with PR depression
options.c: Peaked T waves alone in the precordial leads with a flat ST
options.d: ST elevation in two non-contiguous leads such as II and V2

distractorExplanations.b: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression is the classic pericarditis pattern, not a regional STEMI territory.
distractorExplanations.c: Peaked T waves without ST elevation suggest hyperkalemia or a hyperacute phase and do not meet STEMI criteria.
distractorExplanations.d: STEMI criteria require elevation in contiguous leads of one territory; II (inferior) and V2 (septal) are not contiguous.

options.a: 2 J/kg biphasic for adults, escalating to 4 J/kg on the second and later shocks
options.b: Per manufacturer biphasic recommended dose (often 120–200 J) then resume CPR
options.c: 360 J synchronized, then a pulse check before resuming CPR
options.d: 50–100 J biphasic, the dose used for narrow regular tachycardia

distractorExplanations.a: 2 J/kg then 4 J/kg is the pediatric defibrillation dosing; adults use the manufacturer dose, typically 120–200 J biphasic.
distractorExplanations.c: VF has no QRS to synchronize to, and CPR resumes immediately after the shock without a pulse check.
distractorExplanations.d: 50–100 J is a synchronized cardioversion starting dose for narrow regular tachycardia, too low for VF/pVT.

options.a: 0.02 mg/kg IV, minimum 0.1 mg, maximum single dose 0.5 mg
options.b: 0.5 mg IV every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg
options.c: 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg
options.d: 3 mg IV once as a single full vagolytic dose

distractorExplanations.a: That is the pediatric atropine dose; adult symptomatic bradycardia uses 1 mg every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg.
distractorExplanations.b: 0.5 mg was the pre-2020 AHA adult dose; current guidelines raised the bradycardia dose to 1 mg (maximum 3 mg).
distractorExplanations.d: A single 3 mg push was older asystole dosing; bradycardia is treated with repeated 1 mg doses to a 3 mg total.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-cardiolo.explanation: If atropine fails, TCP/dopamine/epinephrine infusions per algorithm. Current AHA protocols use the 1 mg dose.

options.a: Irregular narrow-complex atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
options.b: Stable irregular wide-complex tachycardia that may be pre-excited AF
options.c: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia that has not responded to atropine
options.d: Stable regular narrow-complex SVT after vagal maneuvers

distractorExplanations.a: AF is irregular and not AV-node re-entrant; adenosine only briefly slows it and does not convert it.
distractorExplanations.b: Adenosine in irregular wide-complex (possible pre-excited AF) can speed accessory-pathway conduction into VF.
distractorExplanations.c: Adenosine blocks the AV node and would worsen bradycardia; atropine failure moves to pacing or epi/dopamine drips.

options.a: Airway optimization, BP support, 12-lead, and targeted temperature/neuro considerations
options.b: Ventilating at 20–30 breaths/min to bring ETCO2 down to 20 mm Hg quickly
options.c: Titrating oxygen to SpO2 of 100% and keeping SBP near 80 mm Hg to protect the heart
options.d: Removing the pads once a pulse returns and transporting without a 12-lead to save time

distractorExplanations.b: Post-ROSC ventilation targets about 10/min and ETCO2 35–45; hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction.
distractorExplanations.c: ROSC targets are SpO2 92–98% (avoid hyperoxia) and SBP at least 90 / MAP at least 65, not permissive hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Rearrest is common after ROSC; pads stay on, monitoring continues, and a 12-lead screens for STEMI and PCI.

options.a: Aspirin, because RV infarction carries a higher bleeding risk
options.b: Nitroglycerin/preload reducers due to preload dependence
options.c: Small IV fluid boluses, since the RV is already volume overloaded
options.d: Lying the patient flat, since it lowers right-sided filling pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Aspirin is still given in RV infarction; there is no added bleeding risk, and the caution is about preload reduction.
distractorExplanations.c: The infarcted RV is preload-dependent, so fluid boluses are the treatment for hypotension, not the thing to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Lying flat increases venous return and helps a preload-dependent RV; the real danger is nitrates and diuretics.

options.a: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push first, then cardioversion if it fails
options.b: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, repeated as needed, before any electrical therapy
options.c: Prompt synchronized cardioversion (or defibrillation if pulseless/degenerate)
options.d: Transcutaneous pacing at a rate above the tachycardia to overdrive it

distractorExplanations.a: Adenosine is considered only for stable regular monomorphic wide-complex rhythms; unstable patients get shocked now.
distractorExplanations.b: Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes is the stable wide-complex tachycardia option; instability calls for cardioversion.
distractorExplanations.d: Overdrive pacing is a specialist in-hospital technique; prehospital unstable VT is treated with synchronized shocks.

options.a: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV/IO first dose, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg
options.b: 5 mg/kg IV/IO first dose, repeated up to twice
options.c: 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 1 mg/min
options.d: 300 mg IV/IO first dose, then 150 mg

distractorExplanations.a: That is the lidocaine dosing for refractory VF/pVT, the alternative antiarrhythmic, not amiodarone.
distractorExplanations.b: 5 mg/kg repeated up to a 15 mg/kg total is the pediatric amiodarone dose; adults get 300 mg then 150 mg.
distractorExplanations.c: 150 mg over 10 minutes is the stable VT dose with a pulse; arrest dosing is a 300 mg push then 150 mg.

options.a: Increasing intrathoracic pressure to reduce preload/afterload and improve oxygenation
options.b: Raising preload so the failing left ventricle can stretch and pump harder
options.c: Removing alveolar fluid by increasing renal sodium excretion within minutes
options.d: Reducing the work of breathing by lowering intrathoracic pressure on inhalation

distractorExplanations.b: CPAP lowers venous return (preload) to the overloaded heart; adding preload would worsen pulmonary edema.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses CPAP with diuretic action; CPAP pushes fluid back and recruits alveoli mechanically, with no renal effect.
distractorExplanations.d: CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure through the whole breath; that rise is what cuts preload and afterload.

options.a: Flattened T waves, ST depression, and prominent U waves
options.b: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, and sine-wave progression
options.c: Prolonged QT with notched T waves and torsades risk
options.d: Osborn J waves at the QRS-ST junction with bradycardia

distractorExplanations.a: Flat T waves, ST depression, and U waves are the hypokalemia pattern, the opposite electrolyte disturbance.
distractorExplanations.c: A long QT with torsades risk points to hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, or drugs, not to high potassium.
distractorExplanations.d: Osborn (J) waves are the classic ECG sign of hypothermia, not of hyperkalemia.

options.a: Synchronized cardioversion at 50–100 J as the first step in a stable patient
options.b: Amiodarone 300 mg IV push, as used for refractory VF
options.c: Adenosine (when vagal maneuvers fail/are inappropriate)
options.d: Atropine 1 mg IV to restore normal AV nodal conduction

distractorExplanations.a: Cardioversion is for unstable SVT; a stable patient gets vagal maneuvers and then adenosine first.
distractorExplanations.b: 300 mg IV push is the cardiac-arrest amiodarone dose, not a first-line treatment for stable SVT.
distractorExplanations.d: Atropine speeds AV conduction and treats bradycardia; it would not terminate re-entrant SVT.

options.a: The patient is pulseless with coarse VF and a rapid ventricular rate
options.b: The patient has polymorphic VT with a pulse, since synchronizing avoids an R-on-T shock
options.c: The patient has stable sinus tachycardia above 150/min from fever
options.d: The patient has a pulse with an unstable tachyarrhythmia requiring shock

distractorExplanations.a: Pulseless VF has no organized QRS to sync to and needs unsynchronized defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.b: Polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronized, so AHA calls for unsynchronized high-energy shocks.
distractorExplanations.c: Sinus tachycardia is a compensatory rhythm; treat the fever or cause, never cardiovert it.

options.a: Rapid transport/activation of PCI-capable pathways and ACS care bundle
options.b: Transport to the closest ED without prenotification, letting the ED repeat the 12-lead
options.c: Scene fibrinolytic therapy as the first choice even when PCI is within 90 minutes
options.d: Nitroglycerin and a repeat 12-lead in 30 minutes before choosing a destination

distractorExplanations.b: Skipping prenotification delays cath-lab activation; STEMI systems want field alerts and direct PCI destinations.
distractorExplanations.c: Fibrinolysis is the fallback when PCI cannot happen in time; primary PCI within 90–120 minutes is preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting 30 minutes to confirm wastes myocardium; a diagnostic 12-lead triggers immediate STEMI activation.

options.a: Delta waves with a short PR interval, as seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation
options.b: Peaked T waves and widened QRS progressing toward sine-wave/VT risk
options.c: Prominent U waves with flattened T waves and ST depression
options.d: A shortened QT interval with no QRS change until cardiac arrest

distractorExplanations.a: Delta waves with a short PR are the WPW pre-excitation pattern, unrelated to potassium.
distractorExplanations.c: U waves, flat T waves, and ST depression describe hypokalemia, the opposite derangement.
distractorExplanations.d: A short QT suggests hypercalcemia; hyperkalemia shows progressive T-wave, P-wave, and QRS changes before arrest.

options.a: Removing the pads and stopping cardiac monitoring once a pulse returns, since rearrest is rare after sustained ROSC in the field
options.b: Ventilating at 20–30 breaths/min to an ETCO2 near 20 mm Hg and accepting an SBP of 70 mm Hg en route
options.c: Support ABCs, optimize oxygenation/ventilation carefully, treat hypotension, and consider targeted temperature/PCI indications
options.d: Keeping SpO2 at 100% on high-flow oxygen and actively warming the comatose patient above 38 °C to protect the injured brain

distractorExplanations.a: Rearrest is common in the first minutes after ROSC; pads, monitoring, and a 12-lead continue throughout transport.
distractorExplanations.b: Post-ROSC targets are about 10 breaths/min, ETCO2 35–45, and SBP at least 90; this is hyperventilation plus hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperoxia and fever both worsen brain injury; targets are SpO2 92–98% and active avoidance of hyperthermia.

options.a: Avoid popping clots with excessive fluids before surgical hemorrhage control
options.b: Raise SBP above 120 mm Hg with large crystalloid boluses before transport
options.c: Keep SBP near 80–90 in head injury to lower intracranial pressure
options.d: Replace estimated blood loss 3:1 with crystalloid to restore normal vitals on scene

distractorExplanations.b: Normalizing BP with big crystalloid volumes dilutes clotting factors and pops clots, the opposite of permissive hypotension.
distractorExplanations.c: Permissive hypotension is contraindicated in TBI; head-injured patients need SBP at least 110 to protect cerebral perfusion.
distractorExplanations.d: The 3:1 crystalloid rule is outdated; balanced resuscitation limits crystalloid and favors blood products.

options.a: Dissolve microvascular clots, as alteplase does in ischemic stroke
options.b: Inhibit fibrinolysis and reduce hemorrhage mortality when given early
options.c: Reverse warfarin anticoagulation in trauma by replacing clotting factors
options.d: Reduce mortality most when started more than 3 hours after injury

distractorExplanations.a: Alteplase is a fibrinolytic; TXA is the opposite, an antifibrinolytic that stabilizes clots already formed.
distractorExplanations.c: Warfarin reversal uses vitamin K, PCC, or plasma; TXA blocks plasminogen activation and replaces no factors.
distractorExplanations.d: CRASH-2 found benefit only within 3 hours; TXA started after 3 hours was associated with higher bleeding deaths.

options.a: Hypotension with tachycardia and cool, pale skin below the injury
options.b: Hypertension with bradycardia and irregular respirations after head injury
options.c: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin after spinal cord injury
options.d: Hypotension with wheezing, urticaria, and flushed skin after an exposure

distractorExplanations.a: Tachycardia with cool pale skin is hypovolemic shock; neurogenic shock loses sympathetic tone, so HR is slow and skin warm.
distractorExplanations.b: That is Cushing's triad from rising intracranial pressure, not the hypotensive picture of neurogenic shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Wheezing, hives, and flushing after an exposure describe anaphylactic shock, not spinal cord injury.

options.a: Phenytoin loading IV as the first-line drug before any benzodiazepine
options.b: Dextrose 50% for every seizing patient before checking the glucose
options.c: Haloperidol IM to control the motor activity and agitation
options.d: Benzodiazepines per protocol (eg, midazolam/lorazepam/diazepam)

distractorExplanations.a: Phenytoin/fosphenytoin is a second-line agent after benzodiazepines fail; it is not the first drug for status epilepticus.
distractorExplanations.b: Dextrose treats documented hypoglycemia; blood glucose is checked first, and benzodiazepines stop the seizure itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Haloperidol is an antipsychotic for agitation and can lower the seizure threshold; it does not terminate seizures.

options.a: Hyperglycemia, dehydration, and Kussmaul respirations with metabolic acidosis
options.b: Hyperglycemia above 600 mg/dL with no ketones and no Kussmaul breathing
options.c: Hypoglycemia with diaphoresis, tremor, and slow shallow respirations
options.d: Hyperglycemia with metabolic alkalosis from vomiting and slow breathing

distractorExplanations.b: Very high glucose without ketosis or Kussmaul breathing describes HHS, the type 2 counterpart to DKA.
distractorExplanations.c: Sweating, tremor, and low glucose are hypoglycemia; DKA is high glucose with deep rapid acidotic breathing.
distractorExplanations.d: DKA produces metabolic acidosis with compensatory deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, not alkalosis with slow breaths.

options.a: Diphenhydramine IV first, adding epinephrine only if hives spread
options.b: Epinephrine IM (and IV/IO escalation per protocol if refractory)
options.c: Methylprednisolone IV to stop the reaction within minutes
options.d: Epinephrine 1 mg IV push (0.1 mg/mL) as the first dose with a pulse

distractorExplanations.a: Antihistamines are adjuncts that do not reverse airway edema or shock; IM epinephrine comes first without delay.
distractorExplanations.c: Steroids take hours to act and are adjuncts at best; they do not treat the acute vasodilation or bronchospasm.
distractorExplanations.d: 1 mg IV push is the cardiac-arrest dose; in a patient with a pulse it can cause dysrhythmias and severe hypertension.

options.a: Hypovolemic shock with hypotension, tachycardia, and rapid breathing
options.b: Neurogenic shock with hypotension, bradycardia, and warm skin
options.c: Rising ICP with hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations
options.d: Sympathomimetic toxicity with hypertension, tachycardia, and fever

distractorExplanations.a: Hypovolemia shows low BP and fast HR, the opposite of Cushing's rising BP with bradycardia.
distractorExplanations.b: Neurogenic shock shares the bradycardia but has hypotension; Cushing's reflex has hypertension and abnormal breathing.
distractorExplanations.d: Stimulant toxicity raises BP with tachycardia; Cushing's reflex pairs hypertension with bradycardia from ICP.

options.a: TBSA including superficial burns, plus the patient's age
options.b: Patient weight and urine output over the first hour only
options.c: Partial-thickness burn depth and heart rate on arrival
options.d: TBSA burned and patient weight (and timing from injury)

distractorExplanations.a: Parkland counts only partial- and full-thickness burns; superficial burns are excluded and age is not in the formula.
distractorExplanations.b: Urine output is used to titrate fluids after they start, but the Parkland calculation itself needs %TBSA and weight.
distractorExplanations.c: Heart rate is not part of Parkland; the formula is 4 mL × kg × %TBSA, half in the first 8 hours from injury.

options.a: Infection suspicion plus vital sign/perfusion abnormalities
options.b: Fever above 38.5 °C alone, even with normal vital signs and mentation
options.c: Hypotension and tachycardia after trauma, without any infection concern
options.d: A positive blood culture result before any prehospital alert is made

distractorExplanations.b: Fever by itself is not a sepsis alert; criteria need infection plus abnormal vitals, perfusion, or mentation.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypotension after trauma without infection points to hemorrhagic shock; sepsis requires a suspected infection.
distractorExplanations.d: Cultures take days and are drawn in hospital; prehospital sepsis alerts rely on clinical suspicion plus vitals.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-trauma-m.explanation: Prehospital sepsis recognition speeds door-to-treatment. Hospitals then deliver early fluids, cultures, and antibiotics.

options.a: Unilateral absent breath sounds with late tracheal deviation and JVD
options.b: Muffled heart sounds, JVD, and hypotension (Beck's triad)
options.c: Flat neck veins with hypotension and clear bilateral breath sounds
options.d: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations (Cushing's triad)

distractorExplanations.a: Unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation are hallmarks of tension pneumothorax, not tamponade.
distractorExplanations.c: Flat neck veins with hypotension suggest hypovolemia; tamponade causes distended neck veins (JVD).
distractorExplanations.d: Cushing's triad signals raised intracranial pressure; tamponade causes hypotension with muffled heart sounds.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-trauma-m.explanation: Both cause obstructive shock; differentiate by lung findings vs muffled tones/equal breath sounds. Breath sounds usually stay equal in tamponade.

options.a: Cherry-red skin as the reliable sign of airway thermal injury
options.b: Circumferential limb burns with distal pulse loss
options.c: Normal SpO2, which rules out significant inhalation injury
options.d: Hoarseness, stridor, facial burns, or carbonaceous sputum

distractorExplanations.a: Cherry-red skin is a late, unreliable sign of carbon monoxide poisoning, not a marker of thermal airway injury.
distractorExplanations.b: Circumferential limb burns threaten perfusion and need escharotomy; they are not a sign of inhalation injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 can look normal despite CO and airway injury.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-trauma-m.explanation: Early airway assessment/management is critical because edema progresses. The airway may worsen quickly as edema builds.

options.a: Needle thoracostomy/decompression in the correct site plus support ABCs
options.b: Pericardiocentesis by the subxiphoid approach, then a fluid bolus
options.c: An occlusive dressing sealed on all four sides over the chest wound
options.d: A large-volume crystalloid bolus to raise preload before decompression

distractorExplanations.b: Pericardiocentesis treats cardiac tamponade; tension pneumothorax needs pleural decompression.
distractorExplanations.c: A four-sided seal can trap air and create tension; open chest wounds get a vented or three-sided dressing.
distractorExplanations.d: Fluids cannot overcome the mechanical obstruction to venous return; decompression must come first.

options.a: Fever plus a white count above 12,000, which by itself defines septic shock without blood pressure or lactate data
options.b: Suspected infection plus signs of hypoperfusion/organ dysfunction (e.g., hypotension, altered mentation, elevated lactate)
options.c: Hypotension with tachycardia and altered mentation after blunt trauma, even without any sign of infection
options.d: A qSOFA score of 1 from a fever above 38 °C, since a single point activates the sepsis pathway

distractorExplanations.a: SIRS-type fever and WBC findings do not define septic shock; shock needs hypotension or a lactate above 4 despite fluids.
distractorExplanations.c: Shock after blunt trauma without infection is presumed hemorrhagic; a sepsis alert requires suspected infection.
distractorExplanations.d: qSOFA scores RR at least 22, altered mentation, and SBP 100 or less (no fever item), and a positive screen needs 2 points.

options.a: Pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression—flumazenil to reverse the TCA
options.b: Bradycardia and hyperglycemia—high-dose insulin as the primary antidote
options.c: Wide-complex dysrhythmias and seizures—sodium bicarbonate for wide QRS/toxicity
options.d: Narrow QRS with torsades—calcium chloride as the first-line antidote

distractorExplanations.a: Pinpoint pupils are an opioid sign, and flumazenil can precipitate seizures in TCA overdose; it is not an antidote.
distractorExplanations.b: Bradycardia with hyperglycemia and high-dose insulin therapy belong to calcium channel blocker overdose, not TCAs.
distractorExplanations.d: TCAs widen the QRS through sodium-channel blockade; calcium chloride is the antidote for CCB overdose or hyperkalemia.

options.a: Respirations, Perfusion, Mental status
options.b: Respirations, Pulse rate, Motor response
options.c: Radial pulse, Pupils, Mental status
options.d: Rate, Pressure, Mechanism of injury

distractorExplanations.b: START uses perfusion (radial pulse or cap refill) and mental status (follows commands), not pulse rate and motor score.
distractorExplanations.c: Pupils are not part of START; the R is respirations, checked first after the walking filter.
distractorExplanations.d: START does not use blood pressure or mechanism; it sorts by respirations, perfusion, and mental status.

options.a: 1–3 subordinates per supervisor (often 2)
options.b: 3–7 subordinates per supervisor (often ~5)
options.c: 8–12 subordinates per supervisor (often ~10)
options.d: 15–20 subordinates per supervisor in an MCI

distractorExplanations.a: 1–3 is narrower than the NIMS span of control; ICS uses 3–7 per supervisor with about 5 as optimal.
distractorExplanations.c: 8–12 exceeds the NIMS 3–7 range; past 7, ICS adds divisions, groups, or branches to restore control.
distractorExplanations.d: A large incident increases the need for structure; span of control stays at 3–7 and more supervisors are added.

options.a: Approximately 30 × 30 feet of level ground, marked with one flare at the center
options.b: A level area of 100 × 100 feet beside a light pole so the pilot can see it at night
options.c: Approximately 100 × 100 feet (day) of level, clear area with secure hazards
options.d: A dry gravel lot of 100 × 100 feet, chosen so the rotor wash stays clean

distractorExplanations.a: 30 × 30 feet is far below the typical 100 × 100 foot day LZ, and flares can ignite debris or blow away.
distractorExplanations.b: Poles, wires, and other tall obstacles near the LZ are rotor-strike hazards; lighting comes from corner markers.
distractorExplanations.d: Loose gravel and dust become projectiles and brownout hazards in rotor wash; firm, debris-free ground is needed.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-ops-spec.explanation: Secure debris, mark corners, and communicate with crew; night LZ larger often. Exact size follows local guidance.

options.a: Airway, breathing, and circulation checked with hands-on vitals
options.b: Activity, pulse, grimace, appearance, and respiration
options.c: Appearance, heart rate, and capillary refill under 2 seconds
options.d: Appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin

distractorExplanations.a: The PAT is a hands-off visual first impression; the hands-on ABC assessment and vitals come afterward.
distractorExplanations.b: Those are the APGAR components for newborns at 1 and 5 minutes, not the Pediatric Assessment Triangle.
distractorExplanations.c: The PAT uses work of breathing and skin circulation seen from across the room; heart rate needs hands-on assessment.

options.a: Effective ventilation if HR remains low/apneic
options.b: Epinephrine IV/IO if the heart rate is below 100/min
options.c: Chest compressions if the heart rate is below 100/min
options.d: Routine deep suctioning of every newborn for meconium

distractorExplanations.b: Epinephrine is indicated only when HR stays below 60 despite effective PPV and compressions, not below 100.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions start when HR is below 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation; below 100 calls for PPV.
distractorExplanations.d: NRP no longer recommends routine suctioning, even with meconium; ventilation is the priority for an apneic newborn.

options.a: Push the cord gently back into the vagina and have the mother bear down
options.b: Elevate presenting part off the cord, maternal positioning, and rapid transport
options.c: Clamp and cut the cord between two clamps, then deliver the baby on scene
options.d: Position the mother supine with legs flat and transport at routine speed

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing the cord and pushing both worsen cord compression; the presenting part is lifted off the cord instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Clamping and cutting is for a nuchal cord that cannot be slipped; cutting a prolapsed cord ends fetal oxygen supply.
distractorExplanations.d: Prolapsed cord needs knee-chest or Trendelenburg positioning and emergency transport, not flat supine and routine speed.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-ops-spec.explanation: Keep cord moist/protected and maintain elevation of the presenting part per protocol. Do not push the cord back into the vagina.

options.a: Prone restraint with a knee on the back until the patient stops resisting
options.b: Physical restraint first, then verbal de-escalation once the patient is secured on the stretcher
options.c: Scene safety and de-escalation; restrain only as needed for safety with adequate personnel
options.d: Entering alone before police arrive so the patient feels less threatened

distractorExplanations.a: Prone restraint with weight on the back causes positional asphyxia and sudden death; patients are restrained supine or lateral.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong order: verbal de-escalation comes first, and restraint is a last resort when safety demands it.
distractorExplanations.d: An unsecured scene with a possibly violent patient requires staging until law enforcement makes it safe.

options.a: Entering the warm zone in standard EMS PPE to begin treatment during decontamination
options.b: Staging downwind and downhill of the release so responders can watch the hazard
options.c: Treating contaminated patients in the ambulance first and decontaminating at the hospital
options.d: Operating in cold zone with decontaminated patients; don't enter hot zone without training/PPE

distractorExplanations.a: The warm zone requires hazmat-level PPE and training; operations-level EMS treats decontaminated patients in the cold zone.
distractorExplanations.b: Responders stage upwind, uphill, and upstream; downwind and downhill places them in the vapor or runoff path.
distractorExplanations.c: Contaminated patients must be decontaminated before transport, or the ambulance and ED become secondary exposure sites.

options.a: Exercising caution for public safety despite exemptions
options.b: Right-of-way at intersections once lights and siren are on
options.c: Freedom from liability for crashes while on a true emergency call
options.d: Passing a stopped school bus with red lights flashing, with care

distractorExplanations.b: Lights and siren only request right-of-way; other drivers may not yield, so intersections are cleared lane by lane.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency exemptions do not remove liability; a driver who fails to use due regard can be held liable.
distractorExplanations.d: Most state laws require emergency vehicles to stop for a school bus with red lights flashing until cleared.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-ops-spec.explanation: Lights/sirens request right-of-way—they don't guarantee it. You can still be held liable for reckless driving.

options.a: Treat injuries and share suspicions with the parents to get their account before reporting
options.b: Treat injuries, transport as needed, document objectively, and report per mandatory reporting laws
options.c: Treat injuries, and report only if the child confirms abuse when asked directly
options.d: Document the parents' guilt in the narrative so police have a clear conclusion

distractorExplanations.a: Confronting caregivers can escalate danger and delay the report; EMS reports suspicions directly as required by law.
distractorExplanations.c: Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion; providers do not need a disclosure or proof.
distractorExplanations.d: The PCR records objective findings and quoted statements; conclusions about guilt are subjective and inappropriate.

options.a: Chest compressions at 3:1 with ventilation for any HR below 100/min
options.b: Early IV/IO epinephrine before ventilation when the newborn is apneic
options.c: Routine oral suctioning and vigorous back slapping before drying
options.d: Warming, airway positioning/clearing, and effective ventilation

distractorExplanations.a: The 3:1 ratio is right, but compressions start at HR below 60 after effective PPV; below 100 means ventilate.
distractorExplanations.b: Newborn apnea is almost always respiratory; PPV comes first and epinephrine only for HR below 60 despite PPV and CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Routine suctioning is no longer recommended and slapping is not stimulation; drying and rubbing stimulate the newborn.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-ops-spec.explanation: Most newborns respond to airway/ventilation and thermal care; meds follow algorithms. Medications come only after these steps when indicated.

options.a: High-quality CPR with left uterine displacement and prioritization of maternal resuscitation
options.b: CPR on a board tilted 45°, with compressions delayed until the tilt is fully set
options.c: CPR with hands placed lower on the sternum and reduced shock energy to protect the fetus
options.d: CPR with right uterine displacement, since the vena cava lies on the left

distractorExplanations.b: Tilting degrades compressions and delays CPR; manual left uterine displacement keeps the patient supine for compressions.
distractorExplanations.c: AHA keeps standard hand position and standard defibrillation energy in pregnancy; shocks are safe for the fetus.
distractorExplanations.d: The inferior vena cava lies to the right, so the uterus is moved to the patient's left to relieve compression.

options.a: Approaching from the rear of the aircraft so the pilot does not need to see you
options.b: Securing hazards, marking a clear zone, and protecting eyes/ears from rotor wash
options.c: Approaching from the uphill side so you stay clear of the main rotor
options.d: Lighting the zone with headlights aimed at the aircraft as it lands

distractorExplanations.a: The tail rotor is at the rear and nearly invisible when spinning; approach from the front in the pilot's view.
distractorExplanations.c: On a slope the main rotor is closest to the ground on the uphill side; approach from the downhill side.
distractorExplanations.d: Lights aimed at the aircraft blind the pilot; headlights are pointed at the ground or the wind direction.

nremt-paramedic-readiness-check-ops-spec.explanation: Rotor hazards kill—controlled approach after crew signals. Approach the aircraft only when the crew signals.

options.a: The PCR may be corrected later by deleting the original entry and rewriting it
options.b: A refusal needs no PCR narrative when the patient is alert, oriented, and clearly declines transport by ambulance
options.c: The PCR should be accurate, timely, and complete enough to support continuity of care and legal review
options.d: The PCR should record your conclusions, such as 'drunk', rather than the observed findings

distractorExplanations.a: Corrections use a single line-through with initials and date, or a dated addendum; deleting the original looks like falsification.
distractorExplanations.b: Refusals carry high liability and need full documentation: capacity, risks explained, advice given, and signatures.
distractorExplanations.d: Labels like 'drunk' are subjective; the PCR records objective findings, such as an odor of alcohol and slurred speech.
